question: Can local first-order relationships between Transformer weight perturbations and activation perturbations identify a principled steering locus, and can a globally applied post-block bottleneck adapter approximate full fine-tuning or complement LoRA more efficiently than prior activation-editing methods?

key_findings.claim: The paper derives a useful structural analogy between pre-MLP activation shifts and GLU weight updates, but the displayed equations do not establish equivalence for an arbitrary fine-tuning update.
key_findings.evidence: For GLU(h)=W_d(phi(W_g h) elementwise-multiplied by W_u h), both perturbations contain gated and ungated first-order paths. Yet activation steering uses one shared Delta h through W_g Delta h and W_u Delta h, whereas fine-tuning uses the independently chosen products (Delta W_g)h and (Delta W_u)h, plus (Delta W_d)m. Matching an arbitrary weight update therefore requires simultaneous solvability conditions that are not derived; the two expressions do not differ only by the down-projection term as the prose states.

anchors.section: B.1, Simple MLP and GLU gradient derivations

key_findings.claim: The post-block argument is a sample-space least-squares expressivity result, not a proof that post-block steering universally reproduces fine-tuning or an empirical ablation showing that this locus causes the gains.
key_findings.evidence: The oracle is defined as the hidden-state difference between an SFT and base model. Theorem 3.1/C.2 gives the optimal error for a linear post-block map approximating a post-MLP map as a singular-value-weighted sum of squared principal-angle sines between right-singular subspaces. The authors explicitly note that these are sample-space rather than feature-space angles. They do not report the principal angles, oracle-fitting error, or a controlled pre-MLP versus post-MLP versus post-block adapter table. Figure 2 instead plots the MLP-output norm divided by block-output norm (about 0.40-0.70), which does not itself measure the fraction of a fine-tuning update that post-MLP steering can express.

anchors.section: C.1, Proposition C.1 and Theorem C.2

key_findings.claim: The implemented steering method is a trainable rank-r bottleneck module applied to the full residual-stream output of every Transformer layer.
key_findings.evidence: Each intervention maps h to h + W_2 phi(W_1 h), with W_1 in R^(r by d) and W_2 in R^(d by r); the linear variant sets phi to identity and the nonlinear variant uses an activation such as SiLU. Unlike sparse layer/head localization, the default policy applies the adapter globally at all layers. This is an activation intervention in the sense that base weights are frozen, although the intervention itself consists of newly trained weights and is structurally continuous with classic bottleneck adapters and ReFT.

key_findings.claim: At rank 8, post-block steering is close to SFT on average for all four reported model families and beats ReFT, but it does not consistently beat LoRA as claimed in the abstract.
key_findings.evidence: Across BoolQ, WinoGrande, ARC-Challenge, GSM8K, AQuA, and ListOps, the mean deltas from SFT are -0.2, -0.7, -0.9, and +0.5 points for Llama-3.2-1B, Gemma-3-1B, Qwen3-4B, and Llama-3.1-8B. ReFT averages -6.5, -10.9, -4.7, and -2.8. LoRA averages -2.2, -1.7, +0.8, and +0.1, so LoRA is 1.7 points better than the proposed method on Qwen3-4B and wins many individual cells. The proposed parameter share is 0.04% for the first three models and 0.02% for the 8B model, versus LoRA's 0.41%-0.45% or 0.26%.

anchors.section: 1, claimed comparison to SFT and PEFT

key_findings.claim: Under tiny parameter budgets the method is substantially stronger on Llama-3.1-8B, but the claim that it has the best average on every model has one negative boundary.
key_findings.evidence: At 0.001%-0.005% parameters, the best proposed averages relative to SFT are -2.6, -1.5, -2.4, and -0.9 for the four models. On Llama-3.1-8B, -0.9 exceeds the best listed baseline, JoLA at -8.9, by 8.0 points. On Qwen3-4B, however, LoFiT's -2.3 average is marginally better than the proposed rank-1 result at -2.4; ListOps also remains weak for all tiny methods, with the proposed rank-1 variant 13.5 points below SFT on that model.

key_findings.claim: The open-ended instruction and RL demonstrations favor the proposed adapter, but each is a narrow comparison rather than a broad validation of activation-space equivalence.
key_findings.evidence: On AlpacaEval 2.0 after three epochs on about 52K Alpaca-Cleaned pairs, nonlinear rank-16 post-block steering obtains 11.34 +/- 0.48 length-controlled win rate against GPT-4 Turbo, versus SFT 11.49 +/- 0.51, linear steering 11.00 +/- 0.53, LoRA rank 8 10.52 +/- 0.48, and all-layer ReFT rank 16 10.96 +/- 0.43. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with GRPO and GSM8K, nonlinear/linear steering reaches 84.7 +/- 0.5 and 84.3 +/- 0.8 Pass@1 versus LoRA 81.5 +/- 0.7 and base 10.2, at 0.04% versus 0.52% parameters. The RL study is one model/task and omits the already published EMNLP 2025 bias-only steering baseline that trains one vector per layer with RL.

key_findings.claim: Joint adaptation has complementary capacity in the simplified fixed-feature model, but one appendix proof contains an algebraic inversion error and the empirical gains are mixed.
key_findings.evidence: For g-hat(x)=(I+delta_h)(x+(W+delta_W)F(x)), jointly changing the skip and feature coefficients can represent combinations unavailable to either restricted component. In the constructive proof, after setting delta_h=A-I, the paper uses (A-I)^(-1)B-W for delta_W; expanding the displayed model shows the required inverse is A^(-1), because I+delta_h=A. Table 5's orthogonal joint method improves over the stronger of rank-8 LoRA and the adapter by at most 2.3 points in the displayed cells, not an unqualified 3.8-point ceiling gain; it trails rank-16 LoRA in three cells, most sharply by 5.0 points on Llama WinoGrande. The 3.8 figure is recoverable only as the gap to rank-8 LoRA on Llama BoolQ, where the activation adapter is already the stronger individual component.

key_findings.claim: Projecting the activation adapter's output matrix away from the LoRA output subspace produces locally decorrelated shifts, but the evidence does not establish global functional complementarity.
key_findings.evidence: The method forms an orthonormal basis V for the LoRA B-matrix column space and replaces W_2 by (I - VV^T)W_2. On 100 WinoGrande prompts with Llama-3.2-1B, cosine histograms at layers 5, 11, and 16 shift from roughly 0.6-0.9 for naive joint training toward roughly 0.1-0.3 under projection; W_2 spectral norms remain 0.8-1.4 across layers. The paper does not specify projection frequency or optimizer-state treatment, and parameter-space orthogonality at one local output does not guarantee orthogonal end-to-end functions after residual mixing and nonlinear layers.

key_findings.claim: The reported small average gaps are not fully supported by a symmetric uncertainty and reproducibility audit.
key_findings.evidence: Adaptation results are means of five runs after selecting one of five learning rates, but SFT is a single run. Appendix standard-deviation tables cover BoolQ, WinoGrande, GSM8K, and ListOps while omitting ARC-Challenge and AQuA even though both enter the six-task averages. Chosen-learning-rate tables likewise omit those two tasks. The 4B tiny-adapter sweep lists 7e-3 between 5e-4 and 1e-3, while the selected Qwen values use 7e-4, strongly suggesting a consequential typo. No paired test or confidence interval is given for the 0.1-0.9 point distinctions.

method.core_idea: Use a local perturbation analysis of Transformer GLUs to motivate learning low-rank transformations of the post-block residual stream, then combine those activation adapters with LoRA while projecting their output subspaces apart.
method.mechanism: At each Transformer layer, a learned bottleneck adapter adds W_2 phi(W_1 h) after the residual/skip path has been recombined, with linear or SiLU variants and usually rank 8. The adapter is installed at every layer. For joint adaptation, a LoRA weight update is trained simultaneously and the adapter's output projector W_2 is projected onto the orthogonal complement of the LoRA B-matrix column space. The motivating analysis compares Taylor expansions of GLU activation and weight perturbations, introduces an SFT hidden-state oracle, derives a least-squares principal-angle error for post-block imitation of post-MLP updates, and analyzes early MSE gradient directions for joint training.
assumptions: Activation and weight perturbations are small enough that second-order and higher terms can be neglected.

For arbitrary fine-tuning imitation, one activation shift can simultaneously reproduce the effects of independent gate and value weight updates, although this solvability condition is not established.
The SFT hidden-state difference is close to a low-rank linear function of the base hidden state at every layer.
Layerwise oracle matching is a sound surrogate for end-to-end sequence loss despite interactions among adapters across depth and tokens.
The right-singular sample subspaces of post-MLP targets and post-block inputs have small principal angles on relevant data.
A global all-layer intervention policy is preferable to sparse learned localization for the evaluated tasks and scales.
Trainable-parameter percentage is an adequate efficiency proxy despite persistent inference modules and unreported activation, optimizer, latency, and memory costs.
In the fixed-feature joint model, F cannot already reproduce the identity/skip directions needed for the task, so activation and weight updates supply complementary capacity.
Early MSE singular directions predict the behavior of low-rank adapters trained with cross-entropy or GRPO over full networks.
Orthogonality between W_2 and the LoRA B column spaces remains enforced as both matrices train and produces meaningful functional rather than merely parameter-space diversity.
Five-run means for adapters can be compared fairly with a single selected SFT run, and omitted uncertainty on two tasks does not change the aggregate conclusions.

techniques.role: Compares activation and weight changes along gated, value, and down-projection paths.
Defines the exact layerwise target difference between fully tuned and base hidden states.
Bounds linear post-block imitation error through sample-space singular subspace alignment.
Adds a rank-r learned transformation after every block's residual stream is recombined.
Tests whether nonlinear adapter capacity materially improves the first-order linear design.
Trains base-weight low-rank updates and residual-stream adapters simultaneously.
Projects the activation output matrix away from the LoRA output projector to reduce redundancy.
Measures local cosine similarity between LoRA-induced and adapter-induced output changes.
Reduces the intervention to one learned vector or rank-1 map for 0.001%-0.005% regimes.

evaluations.setting: Llama-3.2-1B, Gemma-3-1B, Qwen3-4B, and Llama-3.1-8B on BoolQ, WinoGrande, ARC-Challenge, GSM8K, AQuA, and ListOps; rank-8 linear post-block adapter and ReFT, rank-8 LoRA; five runs for adapters after five-value learning-rate selection, one SFT run.
evaluations.metric: Task accuracy and unweighted six-task average difference in percentage points relative to SFT; trainable parameter percentage.
evaluations.result: Post-block averages are -0.2, -0.7, -0.9, and +0.5, versus ReFT -6.5, -10.9, -4.7, -2.8 and LoRA -2.2, -1.7, +0.8, +0.1. Proposed parameters are 0.04%, 0.04%, 0.04%, and 0.02%; LoRA uses 0.45%, 0.45%, 0.41%, and 0.26%.
evaluations.baseline: Full SFT, LoRA, and parameter-matched all-layer ReFT.

evaluations.setting: The same four model families and six tasks under 0.001%-0.007% budgets, comparing one-vector and rank-1 post-block steering with LoFiT and JoLA.
evaluations.metric: Task accuracy and average difference from SFT.
evaluations.result: Best proposed averages are -2.6, -1.5, -2.4, and -0.9. The 8B result beats the best baseline by 8.0 points, while Qwen3-4B LoFiT (-2.3) narrowly beats proposed rank 1 (-2.4). Proposed Qwen rank 1 remains -13.5 on ListOps.

evaluations.setting: Llama-3.1-8B instruction-tuned on about 52K Alpaca-Cleaned pairs for three epochs and evaluated on 805 AlpacaEval 2.0 instructions against GPT-4 Turbo.
evaluations.metric: Length-controlled win rate (%) with reported standard error.
evaluations.result: SFT 11.49 +/- 0.51; nonlinear post-block rank 16 11.34 +/- 0.48; linear post-block 11.00 +/- 0.53; LoRA rank 8 10.52 +/- 0.48; LoRA rank 16 9.59 +/- 0.40; all-layer ReFT rank 16 10.96 +/- 0.43; sparse published-style ReFT rank 4 9.50 +/- 0.49.
evaluations.baseline: Full SFT, two LoRA ranks, and sparse/all-layer ReFT.

evaluations.setting: GRPO on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B for GSM8K with rank 8, sequence length 512, completion length 1,025, batch 6, gradient accumulation 4, six rollout generations, 12 learning rates, and three random seeds.
evaluations.metric: GSM8K Pass@1 and trainable parameter percentage.
evaluations.result: Base 10.2; LoRA 81.5 +/- 0.7 at 0.52%; nonlinear post-block 84.7 +/- 0.5 and linear post-block 84.3 +/- 0.8 at 0.04%.
evaluations.baseline: Frozen base and TRL LoRA; no comparison to EMNLP 2025 bias-only RL steering.

evaluations.setting: Qwen3 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, and 8B on WinoGrande, linear versus nonlinear post-block adapters at ranks 8, 16, 32, and 64.
evaluations.result: Linear and nonlinear curves are close and broadly stable for 1.7B-8B. The 0.6B linear model degrades and becomes more variable at high rank. Exact values and run counts are not tabulated for this ablation.
evaluations.baseline: Matched linear versus SiLU parameterization across ranks.

evaluations.setting: Joint LoRA rank 8 plus activation adapter rank 64 (0.79% total) on GSM8K, BoolQ, and WinoGrande for Llama-3.2-1B, Gemma-3-1B, and Qwen3-4B.
evaluations.metric: Accuracy for naive Joint and orthogonally constrained Joint-Orth versus SFT, LoRA ranks 8/16, and adapter-only.
evaluations.result: Joint-Orth strictly beats rank-16 LoRA in five of nine cells and ties one more, and it improves over the stronger rank-8 component by at most 2.3 points. It regresses versus rank-16 LoRA on Llama GSM8K (31.1/31.2), Llama WinoGrande (59.3/64.3), and Gemma WinoGrande (50.9/51.8), with Gemma BoolQ tied at 84.8.
evaluations.baseline: SFT, LoRA rank 8, LoRA rank 16, activation adapter rank 64, and unconstrained joint training.

evaluations.setting: One hundred WinoGrande prompts on Llama-3.2-1B, local shifts at layers 5, 11, and 16 after naive or orthogonally constrained joint training.
evaluations.metric: Cosine-similarity histograms between activation-adapter and LoRA-induced MLP output shifts; W_2 spectral norm by layer.
evaluations.result: Naive cosine mass is high (roughly 0.6-0.9), while projected cosine mass is closer to zero (roughly 0.1-0.3). W_2 spectral norms remain about 0.8-1.4. No downstream ablation varies the projection schedule or compares functional-rank controls.
evaluations.baseline: Naive joint training without output-subspace projection.

limitations: [Author-stated] The theoretical relationship is local and first-order and may fail for large perturbations or dominant higher-order effects.
[Author-stated] The empirical method changes both the locus (post-block) and scope (all layers), so the experiments do not disentangle where to intervene from how broadly to intervene.

[Author-stated] The evaluation covers a moderate task/model set, focuses mainly on accuracy and parameter count, and does not comprehensively measure latency, memory, distribution shift, or other side effects.

[Reviewer-inferred] The central GLU equations are structurally analogous but do not give a mapping from arbitrary independent weight updates to a single activation shift; the shared Delta h simultaneous-solvability requirement is unaddressed.
[Reviewer-inferred] The post-block theorem is conditional on dataset row-space geometry that is neither measured nor validated by an oracle-fit experiment.
[Reviewer-inferred] No controlled experiment holds rank, scope, token positions, initialization, and optimization fixed while moving the same adapter among pre-MLP, post-MLP, and post-block sites.

[Reviewer-inferred] The learned bottleneck consists of new weight matrices and closely resembles classic Transformer adapters and ReFT, so the boundary between activation-space adaptation and adapter-based PEFT is partly terminological rather than computational.

[Reviewer-inferred] SFT is one run while adaptation methods are five-run means; ARC-Challenge and AQuA uncertainties and selected learning rates are absent even though they contribute to the averages.

[Reviewer-inferred] The constructive proof of Proposition C.3 uses (A-I)^(-1) after setting delta_h=A-I, but expansion requires A^(-1); the intended expressivity statement is repairable only under invertibility of A.

[Reviewer-inferred] The 3.8-point joint ceiling statement selects the weaker rank-8 LoRA comparison in one cell; improvement over the stronger of the two matched components is at most 2.3 points, and stronger rank-16 LoRA wins several cells.
[Reviewer-inferred] Orthogonalization frequency, numerical method, interaction with AdamW state, and behavior as the LoRA B matrix changes are not specified.
[Reviewer-inferred] Parameter-space output orthogonality is tested functionally on only 100 prompts, one dataset/model, and three layers; it need not persist after nonlinear downstream composition.
[Reviewer-inferred] The 4B tiny-adapter learning-rate grid contains a likely 7e-3 versus 7e-4 typo, and two main-table tasks lack chosen hyperparameter records.

[Reviewer-inferred] Trainable-parameter percentage omits persistent adapter inference FLOPs, activation storage, optimizer memory, projection overhead, and the fact that LoRA can be merged into base weights for inference.
[Reviewer-inferred] There is no evaluation of calibration, forgetting, out-of-distribution generalization, safety regressions, or free-form quality for the global residual-stream intervention.
[Reviewer-inferred] The RL experiment omits the direct EMNLP 2025 bias-only steering method, which already trains one vector per layer with RL at roughly 0.0016% parameters.
failure_modes: Large learned activation shifts can leave the Taylor regime, making the first-order design rationale unrelated to the trained solution.
No single Delta h may satisfy both W_g Delta h=(Delta W_g)h and W_u Delta h=(Delta W_u)h for an arbitrary fine-tuning update.
If post-block inputs and desired post-MLP updates have misaligned sample row spaces, the principal-angle error remains large even with an unconstrained linear adapter.
Applying a residual-stream adapter at every layer and token can accumulate drift, overwrite useful base behavior, or overfit the narrow training prompt format.
A low trainable-parameter count can conceal higher inference latency and memory because the new bottleneck executes at every layer, whereas a LoRA update can be merged.
Small models can overfit or destabilize as adapter rank rises, as the 0.6B WinoGrande ablation suggests.
Naive joint training can learn redundant functions and underperform either component instead of adding capacity.
Projecting W_2 away from B can remove useful shared directions or collapse effective adapter rank when the LoRA output subspace expands.
If the LoRA B matrix changes after projection, stale W_2 or its optimizer moments can reintroduce forbidden components unless the constraint is enforced consistently.
Orthogonal local outputs can become aligned again after residual additions, normalization, attention, and subsequent nonlinear blocks.
Learning-rate selection and a single SFT seed can make sub-point average differences reverse under a new seed or evaluation sample.
Strong multiple-choice accuracy can fail to transfer to free-form quality, calibration, robustness, or out-of-distribution behavior.
Global post-block steering can amplify spurious correlations in all layers because there is no learned or input-conditional localization gate.
GRPO steering can exploit GSM8K reward or answer formatting without establishing general reasoning adaptation.
reusable_insights: A first-order analogy should be audited for simultaneous solvability and rank, not inferred from matching symbolic path names.
Intervention-locus studies should move the same adapter among sites while fixing scope, token positions, rank, optimization, and parameter budget.
Measure the theorem's actual quantities—principal angles and oracle-fit residuals—before using it to explain downstream accuracy.
Separate activation-space semantics from implementation: a learned activation adapter is still a persistent module of trainable weights with deployment cost.
When combining adapters, compare against the strongest individual component and an individual method with the same total budget.
Parameter-space orthogonality is only a proxy; audit orthogonality of per-example functional shifts, Jacobians, and final logits across domains.
A changing constrained subspace needs an explicit projection schedule and optimizer-state policy.
Report per-task seeds and uncertainty for every cell entering an aggregate, especially when conclusions depend on differences below one point.
Include additive per-layer bias/vector steering as a baseline before claiming a bottleneck adapter is the minimal route to reasoning adaptation.
Efficiency claims should report trainable parameters, optimizer state, peak training memory, inference FLOPs/latency, and whether modules can be merged.
For global residual interventions, add disabled-layer, sparse-layer, random-layer, and distribution-shift controls to identify where gains originate.
open_questions: For a trained fine-tuning delta, how often does a single activation shift solve the gate/value matching equations, and what is the residual when it does not?
What are the measured principal angles and oracle reconstruction errors at each layer, model, and task?
Does post-block still win when identical adapters are compared at pre-MLP, post-MLP, post-attention, and post-block loci under identical all-layer scope?
How much of the gain comes from intervening globally rather than from the post-block location?
Does correcting the A-versus-A-I inverse in Proposition C.3 change any stated conditions or joint-training design conclusions?
Would orthogonalizing per-example functional shifts or Jacobians outperform projecting only W_2 away from LoRA B?
How often is the projection applied, how are optimizer moments handled, and can exact orthogonality be maintained throughout training?
Do the sub-point SFT gaps persist with matched seed counts, paired tests, and complete ARC/AQuA uncertainty?
How does the method compare directly with bias-only per-layer RL steering at the same model, reward, and parameter budget?
What are end-to-end training memory, communication, prefill/decode latency, and serving costs versus mergeable LoRA and classic adapters?
Do global post-block adapters preserve base capabilities, calibration, safety, and OOD behavior after task adaptation?
Can sparse or input-conditional post-block adapters retain accuracy while avoiding every-layer inference overhead?

competitive_landscape.title: Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for NLP
competitive_landscape.difference: Houlsby et al. insert small trainable bottleneck modules into frozen Transformers and reach within 0.8% of full tuning on GLUE with 3.6% task parameters. The target uses essentially the same bottleneck functional form at the post-block residual output, much lower ranks and modern decoder LLMs; its distinctive claim is the first-order locus argument and joint orthogonalization, not the invention of a learned activation-side bottleneck.
competitive_landscape.source_version: PMLR volume 97 publisher record, ICML 2019 (9-15 June 2019)

competitive_landscape.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: LoRA freezes base weights and learns low-rank weight deltas that can be merged for inference. The target instead executes low-rank transformations on post-block activations at every layer and reports lower trainable percentages; LoRA is also the weight component of its joint method, and LoRA remains better on the Qwen3-4B six-task average.

competitive_landscape.title: ReFT: Representation Finetuning for Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: ReFT already formalizes frozen-model task adaptation through learned hidden-representation interventions; LoReFT uses a constrained low-rank linear subspace and reports 15x-65x parameter savings over LoRA across reasoning, instruction tuning, and GLUE. The target uses an unconstrained bottleneck, applies it globally at post-block outputs, supplies a local GLU/principal-angle rationale, and adds joint LoRA orthogonalization.

competitive_landscape.title: LoFiT: Localized Fine-tuning on LLM Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: LoFiT selects a task-specific 3%-10% subset of attention heads and learns additive offset vectors, reporting LoRA-comparable results with 20x-200x fewer modified parameters. The target rejects localization in favor of all-layer post-block bottlenecks, gaining capacity and attention-path coverage but adding persistent work at every layer; LoFiT narrowly wins the target's Qwen3-4B tiny-budget average.

competitive_landscape.title: Joint Localization and Activation Editing for Low-Resource Fine-Tuning
competitive_landscape.difference: JoLA jointly learns which heads to edit, whether edits are additive or multiplicative, and their vectors in few-shot settings. The target derives a fixed post-block/all-layer policy and a higher-capacity bottleneck rather than optimizing locus/type; it adds full-SFT, instruction, RL, and joint-weight comparisons but does not isolate locus from global scope.

competitive_landscape.title: Steering LLM Reasoning Through Bias-Only Adaptation
competitive_landscape.difference: Sinii et al. train one d-dimensional additive steering vector per layer with reinforcement learning, freeze all base weights, and report matching fully RL-tuned mathematical reasoning at about 0.0016% parameters across several models. The target's GRPO experiment uses input-dependent rank-8 bottlenecks at 0.04%, compares only with LoRA on one model/task, and does not cite or benchmark this simpler direct predecessor; its novelty lies instead in the locus theory and joint weight/activation method.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v3 (2025-10-01), corresponding to ACL Anthology 2025.emnlp-main.467

competitive_landscape.title: Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic
competitive_landscape.difference: Contrastive weight steering extracts behavioral directions from opposing fine-tune deltas and reports stronger out-of-distribution control than activation steering before capability degradation. The target learns task adapters end-to-end and studies local expressivity/composition rather than OOD behavioral arithmetic; its claim that activation adapters approximate weight tuning is therefore not evidence that both generalize similarly.

competitive_landscape.title: Belief Dynamics Reveal the Dual Nature of In-Context Learning and Activation Steering
competitive_landscape.difference: Bigelow et al. unify prompting and activation steering through a closed-form Bayesian belief model, predicting additivity in log-belief space and behavioral phase transitions. The target instead bridges explicit weight updates and trainable activation modules through local network perturbations and explores orthogonal joint adaptation; neither theory subsumes the other's intervention regime.

competitive_landscape.title: From Weights to Activations: Is Steering the Next Frontier of Adaptation?
competitive_landscape.difference: This ACL 2026 work supplies functional criteria and a broad taxonomy positioning activation steering alongside prompting, PEFT, and full tuning as a distinct, local, reversible adaptation paradigm. The target predates it and provides a concrete perturbation analysis and trainable method; the later taxonomy reinforces the framing but does not validate the target's claimed arbitrary equivalence or post-block optimum.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first analytical bridge between explicit weight-space fine-tuning and trainable activation adapters, a theoretically grounded post-block intervention locus, and a new joint adaptation paradigm whose orthogonality constraint exceeds either space alone.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper gives first-order GLU perturbation formulas, a post-block versus post-MLP principal-angle least-squares theorem, a simplified fixed-feature expressivity model, early MSE singular-direction analysis, a global bottleneck adapter, output-subspace projection against LoRA, four-model supervised tables, instruction tuning, one GRPO experiment, rank/nonlinearity ablations, and local shift-cosine diagnostics.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Trainable hidden-state interventions, bottleneck adapters, low-rank ReFT, sparse offset tuning, learned localization, and per-layer RL steering all predate this paper. The most defensible novelty is the particular combination of a local GLU Taylor comparison, a sample-space locus approximation result, and LoRA/activation output-subspace orthogonalization. The broader equivalence and optimal-locus language is stronger than the evidence: arbitrary gate/value deltas need not map to one activation shift, the post-block theorem's geometry is unmeasured, Proposition C.3 has a repairable inverse error, and no controlled locus-only ablation is reported. Empirical efficiency is promising, especially against ReFT and on 8B tiny budgets, but not uniformly superior to LoRA or LoFiT and not yet a demonstrated universal activation-versus-weight principle.

verification.passage_check: Read and second-pass checked all 33 cached pages, including the complete references, notation, first-order derivations, expressivity and orthogonality proofs, error-propagation lemmas, every dataset/hyperparameter/training appendix, Tables 1-14, and Figures 1-6. Rendered PDF pages 4-14 were inspected for equations, plots, table values, and section/page mapping. Aggregate claims were recomputed against table cells, and author-stated limitations were separated from reviewer-inferred mathematical, evaluation, and deployment boundaries.
verification.competitor_check: Official current primary records were inspected for PMLR v97/houlsby19a and arXiv 2106.09685v2, 2404.03592v3, 2406.01563v2, 2502.01179v4, 2505.18706v3 (also ACL Anthology 2025.emnlp-main.467), 2511.05408v2, 2511.00617v2, and 2604.14090v1. Titles, canonical IDs, versions, dates, abstracts/method scope, and direct differences were checked; the target was excluded.

reviewer_notes: The local PDF/text artifacts match fulltext_index exactly and the official arXiv record identifies the cached source as v2, revised 2026-03-06. Every extracted page contains text and anchors do not exceed page 33. Exact table values were taken from rendered PDF pages, not inferred from plots; Figure 4 and cosine ranges are explicitly approximate because the paper provides plots only. Two concrete theory issues are preserved: the Section 3.2 prose ignores simultaneous gate/value solvability, and Proposition C.3 inverts A-I where expansion requires A. The 3.8-point claim can be reconstructed only against rank-8 LoRA on one BoolQ cell, not against the stronger isolated component or rank-16 LoRA. Remaining uncertainties concern the released code's actual projection schedule/optimizer-state handling, whether the 7e-3 learning rate is a typo, missing ARC/AQuA run statistics, and unmeasured deployment overhead.
